text: Track 8.1 Hey Mia! That was an interesting lecture about retirement options and whether it is better to retire or keep working under the new state pension law. Hey Ben, yes, it was. It's only right that older people now have the choice to work longer. Just working one extra year can increase a person's pension fund by up to £4,500 the data said. Yes, and that's not all. If everyone over 65 chose to work for an extra 12 months GDP, that's gross domestic product, would increase by 1%. That doesn't sound like a lot, but it's equal to 16 billion pounds for the economy. What do you think Tom? I understand the argument Ben, but where are all these jobs coming from? For me, there aren't enough jobs for the younger generation these days. Surely it's the responsibility of the younger generation to devote some time to taking care of their older relatives. That way they can relax and enjoy their retirement. Tom, you assume that those who have reached retirement age want to give up work. I know what you mean about the younger generation having responsibility for their parents or grandparents as they get older, but isn't what you're saying unfair towards elderly people? Forcing people to retire at 55 may have made sense in the 1950s, but ideas and lifestyles were different from the way they are now in the 21st century. That's a valid point Mia. 30% of today's workers are over the age of 50 and 1 million are over 65. The number of people who continue to work at retirement age increased by almost 300,000 between 2011 and 2014 and the trend is growing year on year. How can anyone say that the elderly don't have a huge role to play in our economy? If someone wants to carry on working and using their skills, it's quite right they should be able to. In some cases, they have a lot more knowledge than the younger generation who can learn from them. I take your point Ben, but people at retirement age, for example, haven't got the skills required for the majority of today's jobs which involve computers, etc. They weren't brought up in a technological age like we were. I don't think it would be fair to put someone in a role they weren't skilled for just because they're older. That wouldn't be fair for the more highly skilled younger people. We need to ensure that people get jobs if they have the right skills. That's nonsense. Just because someone is older than 50, it doesn't mean they are afraid of technology or unskilled in that area. I get your point that the older generation may not have had a smartphone all their lives, but there has been a clear increase in the number of people over 55 owning a smartphone. In 2019, 55% of people aged over 55 owned one according to one survey. That number is significant. What's more, for the first time ever, more women aged 60 to 64 are in work than not in work, according to analysis of data from the Office for National Statistics. Yes, I read that. The number of older women in work has increased by 51% since the government changed the state pension age. Interestingly, the number of working men aged between 60 and 64 increased by only 13% over the same period. Working is a positive choice for older people as it gives them financial independence. Personally, I think it's about choice. Age is, or should be, irrelevant.
